I say: they are like al-kurhah and al-kurh, and al-du'f and al-du'f, derived from sa'a, except that the fatha form has come to be used for whatever is to be blamed in anything. As for the damma form, al-su', it runs in the course of al-sharr (evil), which is the opposite of al-khayr (good); one says: he intended harm to him (arada bihi al-su') and intended good to him (arada bihi al-khayr). That is why the thought is attributed to the fatha form, since it is blameworthy, whereas the turn (dA'irah) is praiseworthy, so its proper form would not be attributed to it except by the interpretation we mentioned. As for dA'irat al-su' with a damma, it is because what befell them was something hateful and severe, so it is correct that the name su' applies to it, as in His saying, Mighty and Exalted: ﴿If He intends harm for you, or intends mercy for you﴾.

The sakinah (tranquillity): sukun is like bahitah for buhtan. That is, God sent down tranquillity and calm into their hearts through the reconciliation and security, so that they would recognise God's favour upon them in making security easy after fear, and the truce after fighting. Thus they would increase in certainty upon their certainty. And He sent down into it (tranquillity) the acceptance of what Muhammad, peace be upon him, brought of the laws (shara'i') so that they would increase in faith (iman) in the laws, joined to their faith, which is monotheism (tawhid). From Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both:

The first thing the Prophet ﷺ brought them was tawhid. When they believed in God alone, He sent down prayer (salah) and zakah, then the hajj, then jihad, and they increased in faith upon their faith. Or: He sent down in it dignity and reverence for God, the Mighty and Majestic, and for His Messenger, so that by holding this belief they would increase in faith upon their faith. It has been said: He sent down in it mercy, so that they would show mercy to one another, and their faith would increase.

﴿And to God belong the hosts of the heavens and the earth﴾: He sets some of them upon others as His knowledge and wisdom require. Among the requirements of this is that He calmed the hearts of the believers with the Treaty of Hudaybiyah and promised them that He would grant them a conquest. He decreed that only so that the believers would recognise God's blessing in it and give thanks for it, and thus deserve reward; He rewards them and punishes the disbelievers and hypocrites, because it enraged them and they hated it.

*shāhidan* (a witness): testifying over your community, as in His saying, ﴿and the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾.

*Li-tu'minū* (that you may believe): the pronoun (*ḍamīr*) refers to people. *Wa-tu'azzirūhu* (and support him): strengthen him with help. *Wa-tuwaqqirūhu* (and honour him): exalt him. *Wa-tusabbiḥūhu* (and glorify him): from *tasbīḥ* (glorification). Or it is from *subḥa* (the rosary). The pronouns refer to God, exalted is He, and the intended meaning of supporting God is supporting His religion and His Messenger (ﷺ).

Whoever separates the pronouns has gone far astray. It is also read *li-tu'minū* and *wa-tu'azzirūhu* [[His saying "it is read *li-tu'minū* and *tu'azzirūhu*" indicates that the reading with *yā'* is the well-known one. The reading *wa-tusabbiḥū Allāh* ... the verse (ʿ) may hint at separating the pronouns.]] and *wa-tuwaqqirūhu* and *wa-tusabbiḥūhu*, with *tā'*, and the address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his community. It is also read *wa-tu'azzirūhu* with *ḍamm* and *kasra* on the *zāy*. It is read *wa-tu'azzirūhu* with *ḍamm* on the *tā'* and lightened, and *wa-tu'azzizūhu* with two *zāy*s. *Wa-tuwaqqirūhu* is from *awqara*, with the same meaning as *waqqara*. ﴿And glorify Him morning and evening﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: it means the Fajr prayer, the Ẓuhr prayer and the ʿAṣr prayer.

The reading *wa-tusabbiḥū Allāh* ... the verse (ʿ) may hint at separating the pronouns.]] and *wa-tuwaqqirūhu* and *wa-tusabbiḥūhu*, with *tā'*, and the address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his community. It is also read *wa-tu'azzirūhu* with *ḍamm* and *kasra* on the *zāy*. It is read *wa-tu'azzirūhu* with *ḍamm* on the *tā'* and lightened, and *wa-tu'azzizūhu* with two *zāy*s. *Wa-tuwaqqirūhu* is from *awqara*, with the same meaning as *waqqara*. ﴿And glorify Him morning and evening﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: it means the Fajr prayer, the Ẓuhr prayer and the ʿAṣr prayer.

When he said, ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you pledge allegiance only to Allah﴾, he emphasized it by way of *takhyil* (imaginative depiction), so he said, ﴿The hand of Allah is above their hands﴾. He means that the hand of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which is above the hands of those who pledge allegiance, is the hand of Allah. Allah, exalted be He, is far above limbs and the attributes of bodies. The meaning is only to affirm that the binding of the covenant with the Messenger is like its binding with Allah, with no difference between them, as in His saying, ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾. The intended pledge is the Pledge of Ridwan. ﴿Then whoever breaks it, breaks it only to his own detriment﴾, so the harm of his breaking returns to no one but himself. Jabir ibn Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with him) said:

"We pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) under the tree, to death, and that we would not flee. No one among us broke the pledge except Jadd ibn Qays, who was a hypocrite; he hid under the belly of his camel and did not go with the people."

[I have not found it in this exact form. In the hadith of Jabir, he was asked, "How many were you on the day of Hudaybiyyah?" He said, "We were fourteen hundred. We pledged allegiance to him while Umar held his hand under the tree, which was an acacia, and we pledged to him. Jadd ibn Qays hid under the belly of his camel." Narrated by Muslim. In Abu Ya'la, by this same route: "We did not pledge to him for death; we pledged to him that we would not flee. We all pledged, except Jadd ibn Qays, who hid under the belly of his camel." This does not say that he pledged and then broke it; rather, it says that he did not pledge at all.]

It is also read *innama yubayi'una lillah*, meaning for the sake of Allah and seeking His face. It is also read *yankuthu* with a *damma* and a *kasra* on the *kaf*, and with *bima 'ahada* and *'ahada*. It is said *wafaytu bil-'ahd* and *awfaytu bihi* (I fulfilled the covenant), and this is the dialect of Tihama. From it is His saying, ﴿Fulfil the contracts﴾, and ﴿those who fulfil their covenant﴾.

They are the ones who stayed behind from al-Hudaybiyya: the Bedouin of Ghifar, Muzayna, Juhayna, Ashja', Aslam and al-Dil.

This is because when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) intended to set out for Makkah in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, as a pilgrim (mu'tamiran), he called upon the Bedouins and the people of the desert around Madinah to go out with him, out of caution regarding the Quraysh [[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, through the transmission of Adam from Warqa', from Ibn Najih, from Mujahid, similarly]] lest they confront him with war or prevent him from the House. He (ﷺ) put on the state of ihram and brought the sacrificial animals with him, so that it would be known that he did not intend war. But many of the Bedouins held back and said: "He goes to a people who attacked him in the heart of his home (in Madinah) and killed his companions, so he will fight them, and they thought he would perish and not return to Madinah." They pretended excuse by being busy with their families and their property, and that there was no one among them to attend to their affairs. It is also recited as "shaghalatna" with the doubled letter. 

﴿They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts﴾: a refutation of them in their excuse, and that what kept them back was not what they claimed, but rather doubt about Allah and hypocrisy, and their request for forgiveness was likewise not issuing from genuine conviction. ﴿Then who could avail you anything﴾: who could prevent you from the will and decree of Allah? ﴿If He intends for you harm﴾: such as killing or defeat, ﴿or intends for you benefit﴾: such as victory and booty. [[Mahmud said: "That is, killing and defeat, or He intends for you benefit, that is, victory and booty." Ahmad says: This verse is not free of the figure known to the scholars of rhetoric as al-laff (the wrapping of two contrasting elements in one expression). The original form, Allah knows best, would have been: "Who would own for you anything from Allah if He intends for you harm, and who would deprive you of benefit if He intends for you benefit," because this type of structure is used for harm, and so it occurs consistently in the Noble Book, as in His saying: ﴿Who could avail anything against Allah if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary?﴾ And ﴿Whomever Allah wills to test, you cannot avail him anything from Allah﴾ and ﴿They shall not avail me anything against Allah; He knows best what you spread concerning it﴾. Similarly is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, in some hadith: "I cannot avail you anything," addressing his kinsmen, and there are many similar examples. The reason it is specifically applied to averting harm is that the "mulk" (ownership/power) is attributed with the preposition "li" in these places, and averting harm is a benefit that is attributed to the one protected, whereas deprivation of benefit is not like that; it is a harm that returns upon him, not to him. When this is clear, the verse is arranged in this way, because both categories share that each one negates the averting of what is destined, whether good or evil. So when they were close, He combined them in one expression, and specified the expression of averting harm, because it is what those people feared, since the verse is in the context of threat or severe warning. It is comparable to His saying: ﴿Say: Who is it that can protect you from Allah if He intends for you evil, or intends for you mercy?﴾, for protection is only from evil, not from mercy. These two verses are cited in the explanation I mentioned, and Allah knows best.]] And it is recited as "darran" (with fath and damm). "Al-ahlun" is the plural of "ahl." It is said "ahlat," on the assumption of the feminine ta', like "ard" and "ardat," and it has come as "ahlah." As for "ahal," it is a collective noun, like "layal."

And it is read: "ilā ahlihim" (to their families). And "zayyana" (was made attractive), in the active-voice form where the agent is Satan, or Allah, Mighty and Majestic; both occur in the Qur'an: ﴿وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطانُ أَعْمالَهُمْ﴾ ("And Satan made their deeds seem attractive to them") and ﴿زَيَّنَّا لَهُمْ أَعْمالَهُمْ﴾ ("We made their deeds seem attractive to them").

"Al-bur" (ruined, worthless): from "bar," like "al-halk" (the perished) from "halak," both in form and in meaning. For this reason it is applied as a description to the singular and the plural, and to the masculine and the feminine. It is also permissible that it be the plural of "ba'ir," like "a'idh" and "uwadh."

The meaning is: "And you were a people corrupt in your selves, your hearts and your intentions, with no good in you," or "destroyed in the sight of Allah, deserving of His wrath and His punishment."

The phrase ﴿لِلْكافِرِينَ﴾ (for the disbelievers) stands in the position of *maqām* (in the place of) the pronoun ﴿لهم﴾ (for them). This indicates that whoever does not combine the two beliefs, belief in Allah and belief in His Messenger, is a disbeliever. He used the indefinite ﴿سَعِيراً﴾ (a blaze), because it is a specific fire, just as He used the indefinite ﴿ناراً تَلَظَّى﴾ (a Fire blazing fiercely).

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth.﴾ He manages it with the management of One who is capable and wise. ﴿He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills.﴾ [[Mahmud said: "He forgives and punishes by His will... etc." Ahmad said: Similar statements have already been made. The claim that what wisdom requires is what has been mentioned is arbitrary. Moreover, the decisive textual proofs of the Shari'ah come to match what he believes, leaving nothing behind and sparing nothing. How many proofs show that forgiveness is not contingent upon repentance! And how often does he seek to make the Qur'an follow his corrupt opinion, restricting what is absolute and confining what is broad. And Allah is the Granter of success.]] His will follows His wisdom, and His wisdom is forgiveness for the one who repents and punishment for the one who persists. ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ His mercy precedes His wrath, since He expiates bad deeds by avoiding major sins and forgives major sins through repentance.

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Kashshaf, on Surah 48, verse 15:

﴿Those who stayed behind will say, when you set out to take spoils, "Let us follow you." They want to change the word of Allah.﴾ The ones who stayed behind (al-mukhallafun) are those who stayed away from al-Hudaybiyyah. "When you set out to take spoils" means to the spoils of Khaybar. "They want to change the word of Allah" (an yubaddilu kalama Allah). It is also recited as "kalam Allah" (the word of Allah), "to change the promise of Allah" to the people of al-Hudaybiyyah. That is because He had promised them that He would compensate them with the spoils of Khaybar in place of the spoils of Makkah.

[[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "What is meant by the word of Allah is His promise to the people of al-Hudaybiyyah of the spoils of Khaybar as compensation for what they had missed of the spoils of Makkah..." etc.

Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: The first shift (idrab) is then the known one, and the second is the strange and sweet one, in which there is no contradiction between the first and the second, but rather a clear addition and firm emphasis. The reason the second attribution to them is more severe than the first is that the first is an attribution of ignorance concerning a specific matter, namely their ascribing envy to the believers, while the second is an attribution of ignorance in an absolute sense, and of little understanding in general terms.]] That is, when they return having made a truce, not obtaining anything from them.

It is said that the phrase refers to His saying, ﴿You will never go out with me, ever.﴾ ﴿They envy us﴾ that we should obtain some of the spoils with you. It is read with a damma and with a kasra on the sin (tahsudunana / tahsudūnanā variants, i.e., "tahsudūna" with damma or kasra). ﴿They understand little.﴾ That is, they do not understand except a little understanding, which is their shrewdness in worldly affairs without matters of religion, as in His saying, ﴿They know an outward aspect of the life of this world﴾ (Qur'an 30:7).

If you ask: what is the difference between the two particles of idrab (ibtal, shift)? I say: The first is an idrab whose meaning is a rejection that the ruling of Allah be that they should not follow them, and an affirmation of envy. The second is an idrab away from describing them by attributing envy to the believers, to describing them with something graver than that, which is ignorance and little understanding.

Say to those who stayed behind: "You will be called against a people of great might; you will fight them, or they will submit." They are those who stayed behind from al-Hudaybiyah. "A people of great might": this means the Banu Hanifah, the people of Musaylimah, and the apostates whom Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) fought. For the polytheist Arabs and the apostates, only Islam or the sword is accepted from them according to Abu Hanifah, whereas from the polytheists of non-Arabs and the People of the Book, others than them, [acceptance is possible]. The Magians (al-Majus) are accepted to pay the jizyah (poll tax). According to al-Shafi'i, the jizyah is accepted only from the People of the Book and the Magians, not from the polytheists of non-Arabs or Arabs. This is evidence for the imamate (leadership) of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), for they were not called to war during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but after his death. How could the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) call them, given the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So say, "You will never go out with me, and you will never fight an enemy with me"﴾?

It has also been said: they are Persia and Byzantium. The meaning of "they will submit" is "they will yield," because the Byzantines are Christians and the Persians are Magians, from whom the giving of the jizyah is accepted.

If you say: Qatadah reported that they were Thaqif and Hawazin, and that this occurred during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)? I say: if that is authentic, then the meaning is:

﴿You will never go out with me ever﴾ as long as you remain in your present state of sickness of the hearts and instability in religion. Or, according to the view of Mujahid: the promise was that they would follow the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) only as volunteers, with no share in the spoils, ﴿as you did before﴾, meaning at the expedition of al-Hudaybiyah. "Or they will submit": it is conjoined to "you will fight them," meaning: one of two things will occur, either fighting or Islam, with no third alternative. In the recitation of Ubayy: "or they will submit" (aw yuslimu), meaning: until they submit (illa an yuslimu).
He negated blame for these people who have disabilities regarding staying behind from the military campaign (ghazw). And it is read: *nudkhiluhu* and *nu'adhdhibuhu*, with the nun (ن).

This is the Pledge of Good Pleasure (bay'at al-Ridwan), and the verse is named after it. Its story is this: when the Prophet (ﷺ) camped at al-Hudaybiyya, he sent Jawwas ibn Umayya al-Khuza'i [[The "Jawwas" in Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shihab is Khirash, with a kha', a ra' and a shin. Summarised from a marginal note. (ʿ)]] as a messenger to the people of Makkah. They resolved to harm him, but the Ahabish prevented them. When he returned, the Prophet called for ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) to send him, but ʿUmar said: "I fear for myself at their hands, because they know of my enmity towards them, and there is no one in Makkah from my clan to protect me. But I will direct you to a man who is more honoured there than I am and more beloved to them: ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan." So he sent ʿUthman, who informed them that he had not come to fight, but had come only to visit this House and to honour its sanctity. They treated him with respect and said: "If you wish to circumambulate the House, then do so." He said: "I will not circumambulate before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) does." He was detained by them, and a rumour spread that they had killed him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) then said: "We will not leave until we engage the people in battle." He called the people to the pledge, and they pledged allegiance to him under the tree, and it was a samurah tree. Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah said: "Had I been able to see, I would have shown you its location." [[Ahmad narrated it from ʿUrwa, from al-Miswar and Marwan, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out in the year of al-Hudaybiyya intending to visit the House," and he related the lengthy hadith. In it is this story, without Jabir's story. al-Tabari narrated from ʿIkrima, the mawla of Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called Jawwas ibn Umayya al-Khuza'i," and so on. As for Jabir's words "Had I been able to see...", it is agreed upon from his hadith.]] It is also said that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting at the base of the tree with a branch of it over his back. ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mughaffal said: "I was standing over his head with a branch of the tree in my hand, warding off [insects] from him. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 48, verses 22–23:

﴿وَلَوْ قَاتَلَكُمُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ [And if those who disbelieve fight you], from the people of Makkah, ﴿ولم يصالحوا﴾ [and they would not make a treaty]. And it was said: [they are] from the allies of the people of Khaybar. ﴿لَغَلَبُوا وَانْهَزَمُوا﴾ [they would have been defeated and turned back]. ﴿سُنَّةَ اللَّهِ﴾ [the way of Allah] is in the position of the emphatic infinitive (al-maṣdar al-mu'akkad, the verbal noun used to reinforce the verb), i.e., Allah has established the victory of His prophets as a sunnah (a settled way), and this is His saying, ﴿لَأَغْلِبَنَّ أَنَا وَرُسُلِي﴾ [Surely I shall prevail, I and My messengers].

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 48, verse 24:

"Their hands" (aydiyahum) are the hands of the people of Mecca. That is: He restrained them from you and you from them after He had granted you victory and dominance over them, and that was on the day of the Conquest (al-Fath). It is by this that Abu Hanifa (may God have mercy on him) cited evidence that Mecca was conquered by force (ʿanwatan), not by treaty (sulhan). It has also been said that this happened at the expedition of al-Hudaybiyya, because it is narrated that ʿIkrima ibn Abi Jahl went out with five hundred men, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent someone who routed him and drove him back into the walls of Mecca. [[Al-Tabari related it from his teacher Muhammad ibn Humayd, from Yaʿqub al-Qummi, from Jaʿfar, who is Ibn Abi al-Mughira, from Ibn Abza.

He said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) set out with the offerings and reached Dhu al-Hulayfa, Nimr said to him: 'O Prophet of God, you are going to enter upon a people who are at war with you, without weapons or mounts.' He said: So he sent to Medina and did not leave in it any mount or weapon without taking it. When he drew near Mecca, they prevented him from entering, so he proceeded until he came to Mina and stopped there. ʿUtba ibn ʿIkrima ibn Abi Jahl came to him, having gone out against him with five hundred men.

He said to Khalid ibn al-Walid: 'O Khalid, this is your cousin who has come to you with horsemen.' Khalid said: 'I am the Sword of God and His Messenger.' Therefore on that day he was named the Sword of God. He said: 'O Messenger of God, direct me wherever you wish.' So he sent him with cavalry, and he met ʿIkrima in the ravine, routed him, and drove him into the walls of Mecca—the hadith." Ibn Abi Hatim also related it by this route, but its soundness is questionable, because Khalid had not embraced Islam at al-Hudaybiyya, and the apparent context indicates that this story belongs to al-Hudaybiyya. Had it been at the ʿUmra al-Qada, it would have been possible; however, it is well known that they did not hinder him there nor fight him.]] Mecca. And from Ibn ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with him): God gave the Muslims victory over them with stones, until they drove them into their houses.

It was read: "ta-ʿmalun" with the "ta" (you) and with the "ya" (they).

Read with (and) al-Hudā, and al-Hudā: with the yā' lightened and with it doubled; it means what is brought to be sacrificed to the Ka'bah.

In the accusative, it is coordinated with the object pronoun in ṣaddūkum (they barred you). That is: they barred you and barred the offering (al-hady) from reaching its place. In the genitive, it is coordinated with al-Masjid al-Ḥarām, meaning: and they barred you from sacrificing the offering, ﴿detained from reaching its place of sacrifice﴾, that is, held back from being sold. In the nominative, it reads: and the offering was barred. Its place (maḥall) is the place where it is to be slaughtered, that is, where it must be slaughtered.

This is evidence for Abū Ḥanīfah's view that the one who is prevented (al-muḥṣar) slaughters his offering within the Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram). If you say: how then did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and those with him exit the state of iḥrām, when they slaughtered their offerings only at al-Ḥudaybiyah? I say: part of al-Ḥudaybiyah is within the Ḥaram. [[Al-Bukhārī narrated it from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ set out performing ʿumrah, but the disbelievers of Quraysh came between him and the House, so he slaughtered his offering and shaved his head at al-Ḥudaybiyah." And in it, from the narration of al-Miswar and Marwān, "that he ﷺ said to his companions: Arise, slaughter, then shave." Al-Bukhārī said: al-Ḥudaybiyah is outside the Ḥaram.]] It is also reported that the tents of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ were in the Ḥill (the area outside the Ḥaram), and his place of prayer was in the Ḥaram. [[Aḥmad narrated it from the narration of al-Miswar and Marwān, in the course of the long hadith. He said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ would pray in the Ḥaram, and his tents were in the Ḥill."]] If you say:

Then he slaughtered within the Ḥaram, so why was it said: ﴿detained from reaching its place of sacrifice﴾? I say: the intended place is the known place, which is Minā. ﴿Whom you did not know﴾ describes both the men and the women together. ﴿Lest you trample them﴾ is a substitute (badal al-ishtimāl) for them, or for the object pronoun in taʿlamūhum. Al-Maʿarrah is a mafʿalah, from ʿarrahu, meaning ʿarahu when it befalls him: that which is disliked and burdensome to him.

﴿Without knowledge﴾ is connected to an-taṭaʾūhum, meaning: that you trample them while not knowing them. Al-waṭʾ and ad-daws are expressions for striking and destroying. A poet said:

*You trampled us with a trampling born of rage,*
*a trampling like that of a shackled camel upon the grown ḥarm,*
*and you left us as flesh upon the chopping block*
*—if only you had spared some of the flesh...*

This is attributed to al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAlqamah adh-Dhuhlī. Al-waṭʾ is placing the foot upon a thing with force, and it is a metaphor for destruction. Al-ḥanq, like sabab, means grudge and rage. Al-harm, with the sukūn, is a type of brackish plant that camels graze; a camel that grazes on harm is hārim. He says: you came upon us, raised above us by your strength and the severity of your force, like the trampling of a shackled camel upon the fresh growing harm, that is, the moist young plant, which crushes it because of its size and strength, along with the moistness and weakness of that plant, or along with its dryness so that it crumbles. He made it shackled so that its blow would be strong, since it lifts both its legs together and strikes with them when it leaps. Or he made it shackled because the humiliated, when able, does not pardon. Al-waḍm is the butcher's block on which meat is cut. The "lau" is conditional, and its answer is indicated by his words "you left us", meaning: on the supposition that you left any remainder here, you left us like this meat prepared for eating. The expression with lau indicates that you spared none of them.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed the last trampling Allah trampled was at Wajj." [[It was mentioned at the end of Barā'ah (Sūrat at-Tawbah).]] The meaning is: there were in Makkah people among the Muslims who were mixed with the polytheists, not distinguished from them and not known by their places. So it was said:

﴿Had it not been that there are believing men and believing women whom you do not know, lest you trample them, and there should befall you because of them an offense without knowledge…﴾: that is, had it not been for your aversion that you might destroy believing people among the polytheists while you do not know them, so that a harm and hardship would befall you through their destruction, He would not have withheld your hands from them. The answer to "lawlā" is omitted, because the speech indicates it. [[Maḥmūd said: "It is permissible that the answer to lawlā is omitted..." Aḥmad said: Their return here is one matter, though lawlā indicates the impossibility of an existing thing, while lau indicates the impossibility of an impossibility, and between these two there is clear contradiction, because lawlā here enters upon an existence, whereas lau would enter upon his statement "tazīlū" which refers to the non-existence of their existence, and the impossibility of non-existence is existence. So both lead to one matter from this aspect. My grandfather, may Allah have mercy on him, preferred this second aspect and called it *taṭriyah* (repetition for renewal), which occurs most when speech is prolonged and the beginning is far off and the end must be returned to the beginning; sometimes it is renewed with its wording, sometimes with another wording that conveys its meaning. Examples of this have already passed. And Allah knows best, and He is the Granter of success.]] It is also permissible that ﴿lau tazayyalū﴾ serves as a repetition of ﴿lawlā rijāl mu'minūn﴾, since both return to one meaning, and the answer would be ﴿la-ʿadhdhabnā﴾. If you say: what offense would befall them if they killed them while not knowing them? I say: there befalls them the obligation of blood-money and expiation, and the evil talk of the polytheists that they did to their own religious folk what they did to us without distinction, and sin if some shortcoming from them occurred. If you say: the words of the Exalted ﴿that Allah may admit into His mercy whom He wills﴾ are a causal clause (taʿlīl) for what? I say: for what the verse indicates and was brought for: the restraint of hands from the people of Makkah and the prohibition of harming them, in protection of the believers among them. As if He said: the restraint and the prevention of punishment were so that Allah would admit into His mercy whom He wills, that is, into His granting of success for increase in goodness and obedience among their believers; or so that He would admit into Islam whoever among their polytheists desired it.

﴿Lau tazayyalū﴾: had they separated and some of them been distinguished from others, from zāla yazīluhu. It is also read: *lau tazāyalū*.

When the unbelievers set up in their hearts a zeal, the zeal of ignorance, and God sent down His calm upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and made them keep to the word of piety; and they were more worthy of it and entitled to it. (Verse 26 of Surah al-Fath, 48.)

Note: the translation below follows the passage as given.

Al-Zamakhshari's commentary on Surah al-Fath 48:26

It is possible that what precedes it governs it (ya'mal fihi ma qablahu): that is, "We would have punished them" or "they would have barred you from the Sacred Mosque at that time." It may also be in the accusative by an implied verb, "remember" (idhkur).

What is meant by the zeal (hamiyya) of those who disbelieved and the tranquility (sakina) of the believers, the hamiyya being arrogance (al-anfa) and the sakina being dignity (al-waqar), is what is narrated: when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) alighted at al-Hudaybiyya, Quraysh sent Suhayl ibn Amr al-Qurashi, Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza and Mikraz ibn Hafs ibn al-Akhyaf, to propose to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he return that year, on condition that Quraysh vacate Mecca for him for three days in the following year. He agreed to this. [[Al-Bayhaqi related it in al-Dala'il from the narration of Urwa concerning the story of al-Hudaybiyya, and in it: "Then Quraysh sent Suhayl ibn Amr..." at length. The story is in the Sahih from the narration of al-Bara' ibn Azib and from the narrations of Marwan and al-Miswar. In al-Nasa'i it is abridged from the narration of Thabit al-Yamani from Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal.]] They wrote a document between them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Ali (may God be pleased with him): "Write: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." Suhayl and his companions said: "We do not recognize this. Rather write: In Your name, O God." He then said: "Write: This is what Muhammad, the Messenger of God (ﷺ), agreed upon with the people of Mecca." They said: "If we knew you were the Messenger of God, we would not have barred you from the House nor fought you. Rather write: This is what Muhammad ibn Abd Allah agreed upon with the people of Mecca." He (ﷺ) said: "Write what they wish; for I testify that I am the Messenger of God, and I am Muhammad ibn Abd Allah." The Muslims were inclined to refuse this and were averse to it, so God sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger, and they became dignified and forbearing.

And the word of piety (kalimat al-taqwa): "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate" and "Muhammad is the Messenger of God." God chose it for His Prophet and for those with him, the people of good and those deserving of it, and they were more worthy of guidance than others. It was said: it is the word of testimony (kalima al-shahada). It is narrated from al-Hasan (may God be pleased with him) that the word of piety is the fulfilling of the covenant. The meaning of its being attributed to piety is that it is the cause of piety and its foundation. It was also said: it is the word of the people of piety. In the codex of al-Harith ibn Suwayd, a companion of Abd Allah: "and they were its people and more worthy of it," and he was the one who buried his codex in the days of al-Hajjaj.

Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on surah 48, verse 27:

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw, before he set out for al-Hudaybiyah, that he and his Companions had entered Mecca in security, with their heads shaved and their hair cut short. He related the dream to his Companions, and they rejoiced and were glad, and they reckoned that they would enter it in that same year. They said: "The dream of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is true." When that was delayed, Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, Abd Allah ibn Nufayl and Rifa'ah ibn al-Harith said: "By Allah, we did not shave our heads, nor cut our hair short, nor did we see the Sacred Mosque." [[I have not found this explained in this way. al-Tabari narrated, through Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, concerning His words ﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth﴾ up to the end of the verse, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Indeed I have seen that you will enter the Sacred Mosque, having shaved your heads and cut your hair short." When he left al-Hudaybiyah and did not enter that year, the hypocrites found fault with this, saying: "Where is his vision?" Then Allah revealed: ﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled for His Messenger the vision﴾ up to the end of the verse. al-Tabari also narrated, through Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw, while he was at al-Hudaybiyah, that he and his Companions would enter Mecca with their heads shaved. When he slaughtered the offering while at al-Hudaybiyah, his Companions said: 'Where is your vision, O Messenger of Allah?' Then it was revealed." And with the same chain he said concerning His words ﴿so He knew what you did not know and made, besides that, a near victory﴾: "The slaughter at al-Hudaybiyah. They returned and conquered Khaybar." He said: "Then he performed the umrah after that, and that was the fulfilment of his vision in the following year."]] Then this was revealed.

The meaning of ﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled for His Messenger the vision﴾ is that He made true his vision and did not make it false, exalted is Allah above falsehood and every ugly thing, far exalted. The preposition is omitted and the verb is made to reach its object directly, as in His words: ﴿They were true to what they covenanted with Allah﴾.

If you ask: what does ﴿in truth﴾ relate to? I say: either it relates to "fulfilled" (ṣadaqa), meaning He fulfilled it regarding what he saw, and in its occurrence and realization it was a fulfilment accompanied by truth, that is, by a sound purpose and a far-reaching wisdom, and that is what it contained of trial and distinguishing the sincere believer from one in whose heart is sickness. It is also permissible for it to relate to "the vision" as a circumstantial qualifier of it, meaning: He fulfilled the vision while it was accompanied by truth [[His statement "i.e. He fulfilled the vision while it was accompanied" is perhaps: "accompanied" (feminine). (Editor)]], on the basis that it was not one of the confused dreams. It is also permissible for ﴿in truth﴾ to be an oath: either by the truth which is the opposite of falsehood, or by the Truth which is one of His names.

﴿You will surely enter﴾ is the answer. According to the first view, it is the answer to an omitted oath. If you ask: what is the reason for the inclusion of ﴿if Allah wills﴾ in the reports of Almighty Allah? I say: there are several reasons. That He attaches His promise to the will, teaching His servants to say likewise regarding their promises, following the adab of Allah and emulating His way. Or that He means: you will all enter, if Allah wills, and none of you dies. Or that it was on the tongue of an angel, and the angel said: "You will enter, if Allah wills."

Or it is the narration of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to his Companions and related to them. It was also said: it relates to ﴿secure﴾, ﴿so He knew what you did not know﴾, meaning the wisdom and rightness in delaying the conquest of Mecca until the following year, ﴿and made, besides that, a near victory﴾, meaning besides the conquest of Mecca, which is the conquest of Khaybar, so that the hearts of the believers might find rest in it until the promised conquest became possible.

Bil-huda wa-dini al-haqq (with guidance and the religion of truth): the religion of Islam.

Liyuzhirahu (that He may make it prevail) liyu'liyahu (that He may make it higher) 'ala al-dini kullihi (over all religion): over the whole category (jins) of religion, meaning the various religions, including the religions of the polytheists and of the People of the Book who deny (al-jahidin).

And God, glorified is He, has indeed fulfilled this, for you do not see any religion at all except that Islam has might and dominance over it. It has been said: it refers to the time of the descent of 'Isa (Jesus), when no disbeliever will remain on the face of the earth. It has also been said: it means its manifestation through proofs and signs.

In this verse there is a confirmation of what was promised of victory, and a settling of the hearts of the believers, that God, exalted is He, will open for them lands and will bring about for them such dominance over regions that they will be able to proceed to them, [such as] the conquest of Makkah.

Wa-kafa bil-lahi shahidan (and God suffices as a witness) that what He promised will come to pass.

It is related from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him: "He bore witness for Himself that He would make your religion prevail."
[[The phrase "innahu sayuzhiru dinaka" (that He will make your religion prevail) is perhaps "dinahu" (His religion), like the wording of al-Nasafi. (Ed.)]]

Muhammad: this may be the predicate of an unstated subject, meaning "he is Muhammad," since the Almighty's words "He it is who sent His Messenger" precede it; or it may be the subject, with "the Messenger of Allah" as an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan). It is related from Ibn ʿAmir that he read "Rasula Allah" with a fatha, in the accusative of praise (nasb ʿala al-madh). "And those with him" means his Companions: "severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves," being plurals of shadid (severe) and rahim (merciful). Similar is the phrase "humble towards the believers, mighty against the disbelievers," and "be harsh toward them" (wa-ghlu ʿalayhim), "with the believers He is compassionate and merciful" (bi-l-mu'minin ra'uf rahim).

It is related from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, that the extent of their severity toward the disbelievers was that they would guard their garments lest they touch the garments of the disbelievers, and their bodies lest their bodies touch them; and the extent of their mercy among themselves was that whenever one believer saw another believer, he would shake his hand and embrace him. The handshake (musafaha) is one on which the jurists do not differ. As for embracing (muʿanaqa), Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, disliked it, and likewise kissing. He said: "I do not like that a man kiss another man's face, or hand, or any part of his body." Abu Yusuf, however, permitted embracing.

It is the right of the Muslims in every age to observe this severity and this tenderness: they should be severe toward those who are not of their creed and religion, and keep away from them, and they should associate with their brothers in Islam, showing kindness, goodwill, the removal of harm, assistance, forbearance, and gentle manners (al-akhlaq al-sajihah). [[His words "wa-l-akhlaq al-sajhah" mean "the easy ones," as stated in al-Sihah. (ʿA.)]]

As for the reading of those who read "ashidda'" and "rahama'" with the accusative: they are put in the accusative of praise, or as a circumstantial accusative (hal) governed by the implied element in "maʿahu." "Tarahum" is then the predicate, and "simahum" is their sign (ʿalamatuhum). It is also read "sima'uhum," and there are three dialects for it: these two, and "al-simiya'." What is meant is the mark that appears on the forehead of the one who prostrates much. His words "min athar al-sujud" explain it, meaning: from the effect that prostration produces.

Both of the two great ones, ʿAli ibn al-Husayn Zayn al-ʿAbidin and ʿAli ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas, Abu al-Amlak, were called "dhu al-thafanat," because the frequency of their prostration created on the places of contact on them things like the thafanat of a camel. [[His words "thafanat al-baʿir": in al-Sihah, they are the parts of its limbs that touch the ground when it kneels. (ʿA.)]] It is also read: "min athar al-sujud" and "min athar al-sujud"; and likewise it is related from Saʿid ibn Jubayr that it is the mark on the face.

If you say: it has come from the Prophet ﷺ: "Do not disfigure your forms" [[His words "la taʿlabu suwarakum": in al-Sihah, ʿalabtuhu aʿlabuhu, with damma, means: I marked it, or scratched it, or left a trace on it. (ʿA.)]]. And it is related from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he saw a man whose face had been marked by prostration, and he said: "The form of your face is your nose, so do not disfigure your face, and do not blemish your form." [[Narrated by ʿAbd al-Razzaq from al-Thawri, from al-Aʿmash, from Habib, from Abu al-Thaʿa, from Ibn ʿUmar: "that he saw a man who bent down when he prostrated, and said: Do not disfigure your form." He means: do not leave a trace on it. I said: "What does 'taqlib suratak' mean?" He said: "Do not change it, do not blemish it." Ibrahim al-Harbi related it from the narration of Abu Muʿawiya, from al-Aʿmash, from Habib, from ʿAta, from ʿUmar: "that he saw a man whose face had been marked by prostration, and said: Do not disfigure your form." Then he said: "qalabtu al-shay' idha athartu fihi" (I turned the thing when I left a mark in it).]] I say: that refers to one who presses his forehead against the ground so that this mark will form on it; that is showing off and hypocrisy, from which one seeks refuge in Allah. As for us, we speak of what occurs on the forehead of the one who prostrates only sincerely for the sake of Allah's countenance.

It is related from some earlier scholars: "We used to pray, and nothing could be seen between our eyes; and now we see one of us praying and between his eyes is the knee-mark of a camel. We do not know whether the foreheads have become heavier or the ground has become rougher." He meant by this only the one who deliberately does this for hypocrisy. It was also said: it is the yellowness of the face from fear of Allah. It is related from al-Dahhak: "It is not the scar (al-nadb) on the faces, but a paleness." [[His words "laysa bi-l-nadab fi al-wujuh": in al-Sihah, al-nadab is the trace of a wound when it does not rise above the skin. (ʿA.)]] It is related from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab: "The moisture of ablution and the dust of the earth." It is related from ʿAta, may Allah have mercy on him: "Their faces became radiant from having prayed much at night," like the saying: "Whoever multiplies his prayer at night, his face becomes beautiful by day." [[Narrated by Ibn Majah from Ismaʿil al-Talhi, from Thabit ibn Musa, from Sharik, from al-Aʿmash, from Abu Sufyan, from Jabir, as a marfuʿ report with this wording. The scholars of hadith, Ibn ʿAdi, al-Daraqutni, al-ʿUqayli, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim agreed that it is a saying of Sharik, which he said to Thabit when he entered. Ibn ʿAdi said: a group stole it from Thabit, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Shubrumah al-Sharikı and ʿAbd al-Hamid ibn Bahr and others. Sahib Musnad al-Shihab cited it from the narration of ʿAbd al-Razzaq from al-Thawri and Ibn Jurayj from Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir, and it is fabricated (mawdu') on this chain. Likewise from the narration of al-Husayn ibn Hafs from al-Thawri from al-Aʿmash from Abu Sufyan from Jabir, and the matter is the same. And it has other weak chains. Ibn Tahir said: al-Qudaʿi thought the hadith was sound because of its many chains, but he is excused, since he was not a hafiz. It has other chains not from Jabir's narration, which Ibn Jumayʿ recorded in his Mu'jam from a hadith of Anas, and Ibn al-Jawzi from another route from him; it is also false by both routes.]]

"That is their description (dhalika mathaluhum)": that is, their wonderful description in both books. Then he began, saying: "like a seed-crop" (ka-zarʿin), meaning: they are like a seed-crop. It was also said: the speech is complete at His words "That is their likeness in the Torah," and then it begins: "and their likeness in the Injil is like a seed-crop." It is also permissible that "that" is an ambiguous indication, clarified by His words "like a seed-crop that puts forth its shoot," like the Almighty's words: "And We decreed to him that matter, that the last trace of these shall be cut off by morning" (wa-qadayna ilayhi dhalika al-amr...).

It is read: "al-Injil" with a fatha on the hamza. "Shatʾahu" means its offshoots (furakhuhu). It is said: "ashta' al-zar'" when the crop puts forth shoots. It is read: "shatʾahu" with a fatha on the ta', and "shatʾahu" with the hamza lightened, and "shataʾahu" with madd, and "shatahu" with the hamza omitted and its vowel moved to the letter before it, and "shatawhu" with it changed to waw. "Fa-aazarahu": from al-muʾazara, which is assistance (al-muʿawana). It is related from al-Akhfash that it is af'ala (aʾzara). It is read "fa-azarahu" lightened and doubled, meaning: he strengthened its support and made it firm. Whoever takes "Azar" as af'al, it has the meaning of both readings. "Fa-istaghlaza": it passed from thinness to thickness. "Fa-istawa ʿala suqihi": it stood straight upon its stalk, the plural of saq.

It was said: it is written in the Injil that a people will come forth who sprout like the growth of a crop, who enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. It is related from ʿIkrima: "It put forth its shoot: by Abu Bakr; it strengthened it: by ʿUmar; it made it thick: by ʿUthman; it stood upon its stalk: by ʿAli." This is an image which Allah struck for the beginning of the affair of Islam and its growth in increase until it became strong and established, because the Prophet ﷺ stood alone; then Allah strengthened him with those who believed with him, just as the first shoot of the crop is strengthened by what grows around it and springs from it, until it pleases the farmers. If you say: "li-yaghiza bihimu al-kuffar" (that He may enrage the disbelievers by them) gives the reason for what? I say: for what is indicated by likening them to a crop, in their growth and their advance in increase and strength. It is also permissible that "Allah promised those who believed" is given as its reason, because when the disbelievers hear of what has been prepared for them in the Hereafter, along with what honours them in this world, that enrages them. The meaning of "minhum" is explanatory (bayan), as in the Almighty's words: "So shun the abomination of the idols" (fa-ijtanibu al-rijsa min al-awthan).

From the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Whoever recites Surah al-Fath, it is as if he was among those who witnessed with Muhammad the conquest of Makkah." [[Narrated by Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wahidi with a chain going back to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.]]
